strengths: Principled and elegant theoretical formulation: By relaxing bounded RKHS constraints to linear functionals under GP priors and employing Mercer spectral expansions for the conditional mean embedding, the authors obtain closed-form posterior moments for causal interventional functions without intractable density estimation.

Insightful diagnosis of prior work: The paper identifies and theoretically formalizes (Propositions 1 and 2, Section A.6) two key failure modes of existing GP-on-RKHS causal methods (e.g., BayesIMP)—namely, spatial basis collapse/underfitting due to non-stationarity of nuclear-dominant kernels, and out-of-distribution posterior variance collapse arising from finite-dimensional approximations.

Tractable training and calibration: The weighted log-likelihood (WLL) pooling trick (Eq. 21) neatly circumvents the intractability of individual eigenfunction likelihoods, and the spectral tuning algorithm (Algorithm 2) provides a grounded mechanism for empirical coverage calibration.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Experiments across synthetic causal graphs, ablations, and a healthcare simulation demonstrate consistently lower RMSE, improved in- and out-of-distribution credible interval coverage, and superior performance on downstream causal Bayesian optimization (CBO) tasks.
weaknesses: Heuristic nature of the weighted log-likelihood: While Eq. (21) provides an analytically tractable surrogate by weighting marginal log-likelihoods by eigenvalues, it is an ad-hoc pooling objective rather than an exact joint marginal likelihood for the observed non-linear feature maps.

strengths: Principled and elegant mathematical formulation: The paper cleverly resolves the long-standing tension between Gaussian process sample-path roughness and RKHS smoothness constraints by using an isonormal GP relaxation on the functional $f$ combined with a Mercer spectral representation of the conditional mean embedding $\mu(z)$.

Thorough theoretical analysis: The appendix provides rigorous proofs establishing the $L^2$ convergence of the representations, closed-form posterior moments (Theorem 1 and Theorem 5), and consistency of the bootstrap-based spectral calibration procedure (Theorem 6).

Precise diagnosis of prior limitations: The paper formally proves why previous nuclear-dominant kernel approaches (such as BayesIMP, Chau et al., 2021b) suffer from basis function decay, underfitting, and out-of-distribution variance collapse (Propositions 1 and 2, Section A.6).

Practical algorithms: The derivation of the weighted log-likelihood (WLL, Eq. 21) neatly circumvents the intractability of individual eigenfunction likelihoods, yielding a tractable objective for hyperparameter optimization.

Convincing empirical evaluation: IMPspec consistently outperforms relevant baselines (BayesIMP, sampling GP, doubly-robust estimators, standard CBO) in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution uncertainty calibration, as well as in downstream Causal Bayesian Optimization tasks.
weaknesses: Computational scalability: Like standard GP regression, computing the exact posterior moments and marginal likelihoods requires $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ operations and $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ memory. While the authors mention that stochastic gradient descent on mini-batches could be used for large datasets, scalable/sparse approximations (e.g., inducing point methods) are not empirically evaluated in the paper.

Non-Gaussianity of the true posterior: As the authors note, the true process $\gamma$ is an inner product of Gaussian processes and thus exhibits heavier tails than a GP. The posterior credible intervals rely on a Gaussian projection (moment matching via KL minimization). While this is practical and performs well in experiments, the impact of this Gaussian approximation on extreme quantiles (e.g., $\alpha > 0.99$) warrants deeper empirical or theoretical discussion.

Parametrization of the spectral measure: The calibration mechanism tunes the spectral measure $\nu$ over a restricted parametric family (e.g., isotropic Gaussian centered at the empirical mean of $V$). In complex multi-modal settings, this simple family might limit the calibration capacity.

strengths: Principled and elegant mathematical framework: The paper tackles a well-known theoretical hurdle—placing Gaussian process priors over functions in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) without encountering sample path roughness or intractability—by relaxing to an isonormal GP over linear functionals and placing spectral priors on the coordinate feature representations.

Thorough diagnosis and resolution of prior failure modes: The paper provides clear theoretical and empirical demonstrations (Propositions 1 and 2, Section A.6) showing why prior work (BayesIMP) suffers from underfitting due to kernel non-stationarity and out-of-distribution variance collapse due to finite-dimensional GP truncations, successfully rectifying both issues.

Closed-form tractability: Posterior mean and variance of the interventional causal effect (Theorem 1) as well as hyperparameter optimization via a weighted marginal log-likelihood (Equation 21) are available in closed form.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across synthetic CATE/ATE estimation tasks and downstream Causal Bayesian Optimization (CBO) on both synthetic DAGs and a realistic healthcare benchmark, demonstrating consistently superior calibration and regret performance.
weaknesses: Scalability limitations: Like many exact GP methods, the inference and hyperparameter training scale as $O(n^3)$ with sample size $n$. The experiments are restricted to relatively small sample sizes ($n = 100$ to $500$). While stochastic minibatching is mentioned in passing, scalable extensions (such as inducing point approximations) are not formally developed or tested for IMPspec.

Monte Carlo estimation of $\tilde{K}_V$ in higher dimensions: Computing $\tilde{K}_V = \int k(v)k(v)^\top d\nu(v)$ requires Monte Carlo integration over the spectral measure $\nu$. While computed once at inference, this could suffer from the curse of dimensionality if the conditioning/confounding set $V$ is high-dimensional.

Incomplete code link in presentation: In Section 7, the text abruptly ends with 'Code can be found at ' without a URL or placeholder, and there are occasional minor cross-referencing slips in the appendix (e.g., pointing to Section D.2 instead of C.2).

strengths: Principled and elegant theoretical formulation: By relaxing the strict RKHS functional constraint and using Mercer spectral expansions, the paper cleanly overcomes severe pathologies of previous GP-based causal estimators (such as BayesIMP's kernel non-stationarity, underfitting, and out-of-support variance collapse).

Closed-form tractability and consistency with established point estimators: Theorem 4.1 provides exact closed-form expressions for the posterior mean and variance of interventional functions. The posterior mean exactly recovers the state-of-the-art minimax-optimal kernel causal estimator of Singh et al. (2024), providing a coherent Bayesian uncertainty wrapper around it.

Clever hyperparameter training and calibration mechanisms: The weighted marginal log-likelihood (Eq. 22) enables joint optimization of the spectral coordinate hyperparameters without requiring explicit computation of Mercer eigenfunctions. Furthermore, calibrating the spectral measure via Algorithm 2 directly targets frequentist coverage, backed by asymptotic consistency guarantees (Theorem C.9).

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated thoroughly across synthetic benchmarks, causal Bayesian optimization (CBO), and a real-world case study (401(k) data). IMPSPEC consistently demonstrates superior calibration error and interval scores (IS95) compared to relevant Bayesian and frequentist baselines (BayesIMP, sampling GPs, continuous DR, ORF).
weaknesses: Surrogate likelihood heuristic: The coordinate-wise additive Gaussian likelihood on the spectral coordinates (Eq. 11) is primarily an operational device rather than a physically realistic model for non-linear feature projections. Although Appendix A.4 derives perturbation bounds under bounded likelihood-ratio second moments, verifying such condition in practice is difficult.

Moment-matched Gaussian approximation: While the true induced posterior process is non-Gaussian (representing an inner product of GP entities with heavier tails, as visualized in Figure 2), credible intervals are constructed via Gaussian moment matching. In settings with extreme skewness or multi-modality, moment matching may yield suboptimal tail coverage even after variance re-scaling.

Computational scalability: Although minibatch training is demonstrated for hyperparameter tuning, full posterior evaluation scales cubically with sample size O(n^3). The paper does not integrate sparse or inducing-point approximations, which could limit application to very large-scale observational studies (e.g., n > 10^5).

strengths: Principled and elegant methodology: By relaxing the strict RKHS boundedness constraint on the outcome functional and leveraging a Mercer spectral expansion for the conditional mean embedding, the authors neatly sidestep the roughness pathologies of standard GPs while maintaining closed-form posterior moments whose mean exactly coincides with the minimax-optimal estimator of Singh et al. (2024).

Thorough theoretical analysis of prior art: The paper provides rigorous theoretical and empirical explanations for the failure modes of previous kernel-based GP methods (such as BayesIMP), specifically proving why nuclear-dominant kernels suffer from basis-function decay leading to underfitting (Propositions A.10 and A.11) and why finite-dimensional approximations induce variance collapse outside training support.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed IMPSPEC method is thoroughly validated across synthetic benchmarks, causal Bayesian optimization (CBO), and a real-world semi-synthetic healthcare benchmark and the 401(k) dataset. The method consistently outperforms relevant baselines in both estimation accuracy (RMSE) and uncertainty quality (calibration error, interval scores).

Rigorous appendices and sensitivity analyses: The appendix contains complete proofs (including L2 convergence of the interventional process, surrogate likelihood misspecification bounds, and bootstrap calibration consistency), as well as extensive ablations on sample-splitting, kernel families, bootstrap replication counts, and non-Gaussian/limited-support data.
weaknesses: Surrogate coordinate-wise likelihood approximation: Model (11) posits independent, homoskedastic Gaussian errors across all Mercer spectral coordinates. Since Mercer eigenfunctions are typically bounded or oscillatory, assuming identical isotropic Gaussian perturbations across all spectral modes is a strong surrogate assumption, although the authors partially address this via the sensitivity bounds in Appendix A.4 and empirical calibration.

Moment-matched Gaussian credible intervals: Credible intervals are formed via forward-KL moment matching onto a Gaussian process. While this ensures computational tractability and exact mean/covariance propagation, it may mask skewness or multimodality in the true posterior distribution of the interventional function when the conditional distributions are highly non-Gaussian.

Computational overhead of the calibration procedure: The proposed spectral measure calibration requires bootstrap resampling combined with grid search over the dispersion parameter. While feasible for moderate datasets (e.g., ~55s on 401(k)), scaling this calibration procedure to massive datasets without further approximations remains challenging.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: quantifying functional epistemic uncertainty for continuous-treatment and function-valued causal estimands (e.g., CATE, dose-response curves) where standard debiased/Riesz-representer techniques are often inapplicable or sensitive to weak overlap.

Principled and elegant mathematical formulation: by relaxing the strict RKHS boundedness constraint to isonormal Gaussian processes and applying Mercer's spectral representation to the conditional mean embedding, the method bypasses the known pathologies of nuclear-dominant covariance kernels (such as spurious non-stationarity, underfitting, and variance collapse out-of-distribution, which are rigorously analyzed in Propositions A.10 and A.11).

Closed-form posterior tractability: Theorem 4.1 provides exact closed-form expressions for posterior mean and variance, where the posterior mean precisely recovers the minimax-optimal kernel causal estimator of Singh et al. (2024).

Novel and computationally feasible hyperparameter tuning: the weighted marginal log-likelihood (Eq. 22) enables closed-form optimization of the conditional embedding hyperparameters by summing over Mercer eigenvalues without requiring explicit computation of the eigenfunctions.

Strong theoretical and empirical grounding: the paper provides comprehensive proofs for L2 convergence, finite-sample surrogate likelihood misspecification bounds (Section A.4), asymptotic consistency of the bootstrap calibration estimator (Theorem C.9), and extensive empirical validation across synthetic benchmarks, causal Bayesian optimization, and the 401(k) real-world dataset.
weaknesses: The surrogate observation model for the spectral coordinates in Eq. (11), assuming independent homoskedastic Gaussian noise across all Mercer coordinates, is an idealized probabilistic surrogate rather than a physically plausible generative model, though the authors partly address this through theoretical misspecification bounds in Section A.4 and posterior calibration in Section 5.2.

The credible intervals rely on a moment-matched Gaussian approximation (forward-KL projection) of the true posterior process, which is inherently heavier-tailed as the product of two Gaussian processes (as shown in Figure 2); higher-order moments and potential skewness in the posterior are therefore discarded.

The spectral calibration procedure (Algorithm 2) requires bootstrap resampling over the dataset; while empirical ablations show that a small number of bootstrap replicates (B = 10 to 20) suffices, this introduces additional computational overhead compared to purely analytical GP inference.

Scalability at inference time remains governed by O(n^3) kernel operations; while minibatch training is demonstrated on n ≈ 10,000, extending the inference to larger datasets without sparse GP or inducing-point approximations may be computationally prohibitive.
